input: Write daily micro-fiction prompts for thirty days

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Micro-fiction spans many formats — a single evocative sentence, a scenario, a character seed, a first line, a constraint-based challenge. The type of prompt dramatically changes how it is written and how useful it is.
Whether these prompts are for the user themselves, a writing group, a social media audience, students, or a newsletter changes the tone, complexity, and framing of every prompt.

Micro-fiction lives in many genres — literary, horror, romance, sci-fi, magical realism, etc. Without knowing the preferred genre or mood, the prompts may feel misaligned with the writer's creative voice.

Knowing the target word count for the resulting stories (e.g. 100 words, 280 characters, 500 words) defines how the prompts should be scoped — a 50-word flash piece needs a much tighter prompt than a 1,000-word story.
Whether the prompts will be delivered on a specific platform (Instagram, a private journal app, email newsletter, printed booklet) shapes format, length, and style of each prompt.
The user may want prompts that build on each other as a 30-day arc, or they may want each prompt to be fully standalone and unconnected — this fundamentally changes the structure of the whole set.
Knowing what format the final output should be in (a doc, a spreadsheet, a calendar, plain list) and whether the user needs them all at once or as a daily drip determines how to deliver the work.

gold.taskDescription: Create a set of thirty daily micro-fiction prompts to inspire short creative writing pieces over the course of a month.

questions.title: What form should each prompt take?
questions.description: Determine the structure of each prompt — e.g. an opening sentence, a scenario, a constraint, a single image, or a character description — so every prompt is built in the right format.

questions.title: Who are these prompts written for?
questions.description: Clarify the intended audience — the user personally, a writing group, social media followers, students, or newsletter subscribers — to set the right tone and complexity.

questions.title: Which genre or mood should dominate the prompts?
questions.description: Identify whether the prompts should lean into a specific genre (horror, literary fiction, romance, sci-fi, magical realism) or stay genre-neutral and varied across the thirty days.

questions.title: What word count are the resulting stories aimed at?
questions.description: Establish the target length of the micro-fiction pieces the prompts are meant to inspire, since a 50-word drabble needs a far more constrained prompt than a 500-word flash story.

questions.title: Where will these prompts be published or shared?
questions.description: Identify the delivery platform or setting — Instagram, a personal journal, an email newsletter, a printed booklet — so the style and formatting of each prompt fits its home.

questions.title: Should the 30 prompts form a connected arc or stay standalone?
questions.description: Decide whether the prompts should build toward a cumulative narrative or theme over the month, or whether each one should be fully independent with no through-line.

questions.title: What format should the final deliverable be in?
questions.description: Determine how the completed prompts should be packaged — a numbered list in a doc, a spreadsheet with dates, a calendar layout, or another format — so the output is immediately usable.
